items.title: Q1 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit II: Poetry · Alfred, Lord Tennyson
items.stem:
Which narrative poem by Lord Tennyson presents the story of a fisherman turned merchant-
sailor who, after a shipwreck, is marooned on a desert island ?
items.explanation: Alfred, Lord Tennyson's narrative poem Enoch Arden (1864) tells the tragic story of fisherman-turned-merchant-sailor Enoch Arden, who is shipwrecked on a desert island for ten years and returns home to find his wife Annie remarried to his childhood friend Philip Ray.

items.title: Q2 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit II: Poetry · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: In "Memorial Verses" Matthew Arnold pays tribute to three great poets.  Who are they ?
items.explanation: In his elegy 'Memorial Verses: April 1850', occasioned by the death of William Wordsworth at Rydal Mount, Matthew Arnold pays tribute to three towering European Romantic-era figures: Lord Byron (passion and titanic strife), Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (sage wisdom), and Wordsworth (healing emotional joy).

items.title: Q3 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · John Fowles
items.stem:
Who among the following English playwrights wrote screenplays on novels such as Marcel
Proust's In Search of Lost Time, John Fowles's French Lieutenant's Woman, and Margaret
Atwood's Handmaid's Tale ?
items.explanation: Nobel Laureate playwright Harold Pinter had a prolific parallel career as a screenwriter, adapting John Fowles's The French Lieutenant's Woman (1981), Margaret Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale (1990), and Marcel Proust's In Search of Lost Time (published as The Proust Screenplay, 1977).

items.title: Q4 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: The years in English literary history between 1649 and 1660 are known as __________
items.explanation: The years between the execution of King Charles I in January 1649 and the Restoration of King Charles II in May 1660—when England was ruled as a republic and Protectorate under Oliver Cromwell—are known in English literary history as the Commonwealth period (or Puritan Interregnum).

items.title: Q5 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · R. K. Narayan
items.stem:
In R.K. Narayan's Swami and Friends, which game offers Swami the best kind of emotional
release from the strains and pressures of disagreeable circumstances ?
items.explanation: In R. K. Narayan's debut novel Swami and Friends (1935), the schoolboy Swaminathan and his friends Rajam and Mani form the Malgudi Cricket Club (M.C.C.), where playing cricket offers Swami his greatest emotional release from school and family pressures.

items.title: Q6 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit II: Poetry · William Blake
items.stem:
William Blake expressed the importance of the particular when he said that "To Generalize
is to be __________.  To particularize is the alone Distinction of Merit."  Fill in the blank
items.explanation: In his marginal annotations (c. 1808) to Sir Joshua Reynolds's Discourses on Art, William Blake rejected neoclassical abstraction with the fiery aphorism: 'To Generalize is to be an Idiot. To Particularize is the Alone Distinction of Merit.'

items.title: Q7 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Which of the following was not a dialect of Old English ?
items.explanation: Old English (Anglo-Saxon) had four main Germanic dialects—Northumbrian, Mercian, West Saxon, and Kentish—whereas Irish (Goidelic) belongs to the Celtic branch of the Indo-European language family.

items.title: Q8 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Anthony Burgess
items.stem:
Anthony Burgess's last novel, published in 1993, is called A Dead Man in Deptford.  Who is
the central character to whom the title refers ?
items.explanation: Anthony Burgess's final novel, A Dead Man in Deptford (1993), is a historical biofiction about Elizabethan playwright, poet, and government spy Christopher Marlowe, who was fatally stabbed in a Deptford lodging house in May 1593.

items.title: Q9 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Shakespeare, William Caxton, John Milton, John Donne
items.stem: Choose the correct chronological order
options: William Caxton prints the first English book - William Shakespeare's First Folio - John Milton's Areopagitica - "Tottel's Miscellany" (Songs and Sonnets)
Tottel's Miscellany" (Songs and Sonnets) - William Shakespeare's First Folio - William Caxton prints the first English book - John Milton's Areopagitica
William Caxton prints the first English book - "Tottel's Miscellany" (Songs and Sonnets) - William Shakespeare's First Folio - John Milton's Areopagitica
William Shakespeare's First Folio - John Milton's Areopagitica - William Caxton prints the first English book - "Tottel's Miscellany" (Songs and Sonnets)
items.explanation: The correct chronological order is: William Caxton prints the first English book (Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye, c. 1473–1474), Richard Tottel publishes Songes and Sonettes (Tottel's Miscellany, 1557), Shakespeare's First Folio appears (1623), and John Milton publishes Areopagitica (1644).

items.title: Q10 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Roman Augustan (Golden Age) · Unit II: Poetry · Horace
items.stem: What does the phrase ut pictura poesis from Horace's Art of Poetry mean ?
options: as in painting, so in poetry
as in poetry, so in painting
items.explanation: In his Ars Poetica (Art of Poetry, c. 19 BCE), the Roman poet Horace coined the Latin phrase 'ut pictura poesis', which translates literally as 'as is painting, so is poetry' (or 'as in painting, so in poetry').

items.title: Q11 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit I: Drama · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem:
Who among the following is the author of Account of the Augustan Age in England
(1759) ?
items.explanation: Anglo-Irish writer Oliver Goldsmith wrote the critical essay 'An Account of the Augustan Age in England', published in the eighth and final issue of his weekly periodical The Bee on 24 November 1759.

items.title: Q12 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Miguel de Cervantes
items.stem: In how many parts did Cervantes publish his novel, Don Quixote ?
items.explanation: Spanish Golden Age writer Miguel de Cervantes published his masterpiece Don Quixote in two parts: Part One appeared in Madrid in 1605, and Part Two was published ten years later in 1615.

items.title: Q13 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit II: Poetry · Robert Browning
items.stem:
Lytton Strachey's Eminent Victorians carries biographical sketches of writers and public figures.
Identify the list below that correctly mentions those Eminent Victorians
options: Cardinal Manning, Florence Nightingale, Thomas Arnold and General Gordon
Mason, Sir Arthur Quiller Couch, Matthew Arnold, Robert Bridges
Benson, Cardinal Manning, Lord Tennyson, Beatrice Webb
George Harding, General Gordon, Robert Browning, Mrs Humphrey Ward
items.explanation: Bloomsbury Group biographer Lytton Strachey's irreverent masterpiece Eminent Victorians (1918) consists of four satirical biographical portraits: Cardinal Henry Edward Manning, Florence Nightingale, Dr Thomas Arnold, and General Charles 'Chinese' Gordon.

items.title: Q14 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · John Dryden
items.stem:
One of the following statements about the eponymous saint of Dryden's "Song for St. Cecilia's
Day" is incorrect.  Identify that statement
options: Cecilia was a Roman lady, an early Christian martyr
Cecilia was an Armenian devotee of the Christian faith
Cecilia's festival is celebrated on 22 November in England
Cecilia was a patroness of music who was fabled to have invented the organ
items.explanation: Saint Cecilia, the patron saint of music celebrated in John Dryden's ode 'A Song for St. Cecilia's Day' (1687) on her feast day of 22 November, was a noble Roman Christian martyr of the second or third century, not an Armenian devotee.

items.title: Q15 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit II: Poetry · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: Which of the statements on Michael Roberts's Faber Book of Modern Verse (1936) is not true ?
options: His anthology canonized modern poetry and poets for quite some decades
The collection begins with the poems of Robert Bridges
Roberts omitted the Georgian poets in his anthology
Yeats, Eliot and Pound find a place in the Faber Book of 1936
items.explanation: Michael Roberts's influential anthology The Faber Book of Modern Verse (1936), which canonized modernist poetry and excluded the Georgian poets, opens with thirteen poems by Gerard Manley Hopkins—not Robert Bridges.

items.title: Q16 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Jean Baudrillard
items.stem:
Who among the following proposed that the First Gulf War had never taken place, it was
simply a hyperreal, media-generated spectacle ?
items.explanation: French postmodern theorist Jean Baudrillard published three provocative essays collected as The Gulf War Did Not Take Place (La Guerre du Golfe n'a pas eu lieu, 1991), arguing that the 1991 conflict was experienced as a sanitized, hyperreal media spectacle and simulacrum.

items.title: Q17 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Julian of Norwich
items.stem: Sir Thomas Browne's Urn Burial was prompted by __________
options: the discovery of ancient burial-urns near Norwich
the contemporary researches on burial rites in Norway
the death of St. Francis of Assissi and his burial
the publication of the English Book of Common Prayer
items.explanation: Sir Thomas Browne's meditative prose treatise Hydriotaphia, Urn Burial (1658) was prompted by the unearthing of forty to fifty ancient Roman/Anglo-Saxon clay cremation urns in a field at Old Walsingham in Norfolk, near Browne's home in Norwich.

items.title: Q18 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Edith Wharton
items.stem:
Identify from among the following list those that cannot be called War Fiction.
(a)
A Modern Instance
(b)
Catch - 22
(c)
The Age of Innocence
(d)
The Naked and the Dead
items.explanation: While Joseph Heller's Catch-22 (1961) and Norman Mailer's The Naked and the Dead (1948) are classic World War II novels, William Dean Howells's A Modern Instance (1882) and Edith Wharton's The Age of Innocence (1920) are realist novels of domestic marriage and Gilded Age New York society.

items.title: Q19 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Philip Larkin
items.stem:
Who among the following writers was not the one identified with The Movement of the
1950's England ?
items.explanation: Kingsley Amis, Philip Larkin, and Donald Davie were core members of the 1950s English poetic group known as 'The Movement' (anthologized in Robert Conquest's New Lines, 1956), whereas Roy Fuller was an older 1930s–1940s socially committed poet.

items.title: Q20 · July 2018 (Paper II)

items.title: Q22 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
From among the following, identify the incorrect observation regarding Ferdinand de
Saussure's seminal distinction between langue and parole
options: Parole is the particular language system, the elements of which we learn as children, and which is codified in our grammars and dictionaries, whereas langue is the language-occasion (what A says to B)
A language consists in the interrelationship between langue and parole
Saussure made this crucial distinction in a study called A Course in General Linguistics

Langue is the particular language-system, the elements of which we learn as children, and which is codified in our grammars and dictionaries, whereas parole is the language-occasion (what A says to B)
items.explanation: In Ferdinand de Saussure's Course in General Linguistics (1916), langue is the abstract, shared grammatical system of a language internalized by speakers, whereas parole is the individual concrete act of speech; the first statement is incorrect because it reverses the two terms.

items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism

John Heywood wrote a farcical interlude called The Four P's.
Who were the Four P's ?
options: Palmer, a Pedlar, a Pothecary, a Packer
Printer, a Pedlar, a Pothecary, a Palmer
Pedlar, a Parson, a Palmer, a Pothecary
Palmer, a Pardoner, a Pothecary, a Pedlar
items.explanation: Tudor dramatist John Heywood's comic verse interlude The Playe Called the Foure PP (c. 1530, printed c. 1544) features a lying contest among four characters whose professions begin with P: a Palmer, a Pardoner, a 'Pothecary (Apothecary), and a Pedlar.

items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
In the mechanical drill method of second language acquisition :
(a)
The learner has the freedom to choose from many responses.
(b)
The learner's response is totally controlled.
(c)
Comprehension of the item by the learner is not required.
(d)

items.explanation: As classified by Christina Bratt Paulston in second language pedagogy, a mechanical drill (unlike meaningful or communicative drills) involves complete control over the learner's response (b) with only one correct way of responding, and the learner can complete it without needing to understand the meaning of the item (c).

items.title: Q25 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit II: Poetry · Henry King
items.stem:
Thou wilt not wake
Till I thy fate shall overtake;
Till age, or grief, or sickness must
Marry my body to that dust
It so much loves; and fill the room
My heart keeps empty in thy Tomb.
Stay for me there; I will not fail
To meet thee in that hollow Vale.
And think not much of my delay;
I am already on the way.

Which of the following readings do you find appropriate to the spirit of the lines above ?
options: In that interspace between the lines, the ending of one and the beginning of another, there is a silent internal language, the poem's language-within-language, tacitly signalled through the deployment of rhymed space.

Ageing and dying are of course helplessly passive; but here love makes them as though they were now also willing things in the husband eager to join his dead wife. Through simple intimate tones of their shared earthly life - stay for me, wait for me, I will not fail - he not only imagines her but imagines her thinking of him.

The lyric voice here can feel the poem speaking back to him - in the cold lineal stare of 'there was nothing in my belief' - even as his dead wife did not. It is as though the poem itself then demands his response, in order to be able to move from one line to another. To attempt that movement in keeping the poem's space alive, the lyric voice asserts, 'I will not fail/To meet there in that hollow Vale.'

My whole nature was so penetrated with grief and humiliation of such considerations, that, even now, famous and caressed and happy as I am, I often forget in my dream that I have a dear wife who died, leaving me alone in this world. Even that I am a man, and now I wander desolately back to that time of our lives when my wife and I shared moments of bliss.
items.explanation: These lines are from Henry King's famous elegy 'The Exequy' (written on the death of his young wife Anne Berkeley in 1624). Love transforms the helplessness of ageing and death into a willing, eager journey to be reunited with his deceased wife in the grave ('Stay for me there; I will not fail / To meet thee in that hollow Vale').

items.title: Q27 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
The very last passage of a novel is given below.  Identify the novel.
"Welcome, O life, I go to encounter for the millionth time the reality of experience and to
forge in the smithy of my soul the uncreated conscience of my race.
April 27.  Old father, old artificer, stand me now and ever in good stead."
options: Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
items.explanation: These iconic diary entries from 26 and 27 April form the concluding lines of James Joyce's Künstlerroman A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916), as Stephen Dedalus invokes the mythical craftsman Daedalus ('Old father, old artificer') before departing Dublin.

items.title: Q28 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · unit-4-non-fictional-prose · Francis Bacon
items.stem: Francis Bacon's New Atlantis is about a utopian state called __________
items.explanation: Published posthumously in 1626, Francis Bacon's unfinished utopian prose romance New Atlantis depicts the mythical Pacific island kingdom of Bensalem, centred on its state-sponsored scientific research institution, Salomon's House.

items.title: Q29 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
The 1950's saw the rise of backlash against modernism and against New Romanticism that
became known as The Movement.  Which of the following little magazines came to be
associated with The Movement ?
(a)
Departure
(b)
New Verse
(c)
London Mercury
(d)
New Poems
The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: The 1950s Movement poets published early work in the Oxford university magazine Departure (founded by John Adlard and Alan Brownjohn in 1952) and in the annual PEN anthologies New Poems, whereas The London Mercury belonged to the 1920s 'Squirearchy' and New Verse was Geoffrey Grigson's 1930s Auden-generation journal.

items.title: Q30 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem:
The error of interpreting a literary work by referring to evidence outside of itself, such as the
design and purpose of the author is called __________
items.explanation: Coined by New Critics W. K. Wimsatt and Monroe C. Beardsley in their 1946 essay 'The Intentional Fallacy', the intentional fallacy is the error of judging or interpreting a literary work by appealing to the author's stated or inferred biographical intentions outside the text.

items.title: Q31 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth
items.stem:

I'd rather
be
suckled by
an
outworn pagan
than
get my horn
wreathed in
an
old triton.
Which poet, which poem ?
options: John Keats, "On First Looking into Chapman's Homer
William Wordsworth, "The World is Too Much with Us
Elizabeth B. Browning, "How do I Love Thee... ?
items.explanation: American poet A. R. Ammons's playfully irreverent nine-line poem 'Swoggled' parodies the famous closing sestet of William Wordsworth's sonnet 'The World Is Too Much with Us' (1807): 'I'd rather be / A Pagan suckled in a creed outworn... Or hear old Triton blow his wreathèd horn.'

items.title: Q32 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Fanny Burney
items.stem: Fanny Burney's Evelina carries the subtitle
options: Naive Lady's Entrance into the World
Young Lady's Entrance into the World
Young Lady's Exit from the World
Bold Lady's Entrance into the Hall
items.explanation: Frances (Fanny) Burney's 1778 epistolary novel Evelina bears the full subtitle 'or, a Young Lady's Entrance into the World' (revised in later editions to 'The History of a Young Lady's Entrance into the World').

items.title: Q33 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Philip Sidney
items.stem: What does Philip Sidney call poet-haters in his Defence of Poesie ?
items.explanation: In An Apologie for Poetrie (The Defence of Poesie, written c. 1580, published 1595), Sir Philip Sidney refers to puritanical detractors and haters of poetry by the Greek compound term 'mysomousoi' (misomousoi), meaning 'haters of the Muses'.

items.title: Q34 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Kamau Brathwaite
items.stem:
Who, among the following, raises the following painful question of longing and belonging ?
"Where shall I turn, divided to the vein ?
I who have cursed
The drunken officer of British rule, how choose
Between this Africa and the English tongue I love ?"
items.explanation: These famous closing lines come from St. Lucian Nobel Laureate Derek Walcott's poem 'A Far Cry from Africa' (published in In a Green Night, 1962), which meditates on the Mau Mau uprising in Kenya and the poet's divided racial and linguistic heritage.

items.title: Q35 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Cleanth Brooks

called "The Intentional Fallacy" and "The Affective Fallacy".

Cleanth Brooks

Monroe C. Beardsley

items.title: Q36 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Philip Larkin
items.stem:
Philip Larkin's "Sad Steps" notices "The way the moon dashes through clouds that blow
Loosely as cannon-smoke to stand apart...."
The poem alludes to
options: The moonlit scenes in A Midsummer Night's Dream
items.explanation: Both the title and the lunar theme of Philip Larkin's poem 'Sad Steps' (written 1968, collected in High Windows, 1974) allude directly to Sonnet 31 of Sir Philip Sidney's Elizabethan sonnet sequence Astrophil and Stella: 'With how sad steps, O Moon, thou climb'st the skies!'

items.title: Q38 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · T. S. Eliot, Cormac McCarthy

(a)
Look, Stranger!
(b)
The Tower

The Waste Land

Code
items.explanation: T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land (1922) and W. B. Yeats's The Tower (1928) were both published in the 1920s, whereas W. H. Auden's Look, Stranger! (1936) and George Orwell's The Road to Wigan Pier (1937) were published in the 1930s.

items.title: Q39 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
This novel is dedicated "To the railroad of bones" and has as its epigraph the line,
"I am the woman they give dead women's clothes to" from Christine Gelineau's "Inheritance".
Identify the novel
options: The Chibok Girls by Helon Habila
The Underground Railroad by Colson Whitehead
The Book of Night Women by Marlon James
items.explanation: Jamaican author Marlon James's historical novel The Book of Night Women (2009), about a slave women's revolt on a late eighteenth-century Jamaican sugar plantation, is dedicated 'To the railroad of bones' and carries the epigraph from Christine Gelineau's poem 'Inheritance'.

items.title: Q40 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth
items.stem:

life-time :

Which poet ?  What "dawn" ?
options: Lord Tennyson ; the Jubilee of Queen Victoria's reign
items.explanation: In Book XI of The Prelude (also published separately in 1809 as 'French Revolution, as It Appeared to Enthusiasts at Its Commencement'), William Wordsworth captured his youthful revolutionary enthusiasm for the dawn of the French Revolution of 1789 with these celebrated lines.

items.title: Q41 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which novel by John Banville tells the story of a group of travellers who arrive on a small
island and stumble upon the house of Prof. Kreutznaer whose relationship to a painting
entitled The Golden World by a fictional Dutch artist named Vaublin plays a central role ?
items.explanation: Irish novelist John Banville's Ghosts (1993)—the second volume of his 'Frames' trilogy between The Book of Evidence and Athena—centres on a group of castaways on a small island who encounter Professor Kreutznaer and the mysterious masterpiece Le Monde d'or (The Golden World) by the fictional painter Jean Vaublin.

items.title: Q42 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Anthony Burgess
items.stem:
Identify the two plays, usually paired for their critique of the politics of language and acts of
police interrogation
options: One for the Road, Mountain Language
items.explanation: Harold Pinter's short political plays One for the Road (1984) and Mountain Language (1988) are frequently paired as companion pieces exposing totalitarian state torture, police interrogation, and the violent suppression of language.

items.title: Q43 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem:
Semiotics originated mainly in the works of two theorists.  They are :
(a)
Charles Sanders Peirce
(b)
Mikhail Bakhtin
(c)
Ferdinand de Saussure
(d)
Valentin Voloshinov
The right combination according to the code is __________
items.explanation: Modern semiotics (the systematic study of signs) originated independently at the turn of the twentieth century in the philosophical 'semiotic' of American pragmatist Charles Sanders Peirce (a) and the structural 'semiology' of Swiss linguist Ferdinand de Saussure (c).

items.title: Q44 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Robert Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy was published in 1621 and expanded and altered in
__________ subsequent editions
items.explanation: Following its first publication in 1621, Oxford scholar Robert Burton continually revised and expanded The Anatomy of Melancholy across five subsequent editions containing his authorial additions (1624, 1628, 1632, 1638, and the posthumous 1651 edition).

items.title: Q45 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · George Meredith
items.stem:
Which of the following magazines self-consciously created an identity for Vorticists, a group
of painters, sculptors and writers ?
items.explanation: Edited by Wyndham Lewis with contributions from Ezra Pound, Henri Gaudier-Brzeska, and Rebecca West, the bold pink-covered avant-garde magazine BLAST: Review of the Great English Vortex (published in two issues in 1914 and 1915) served as the manifesto and mouthpiece of the Vorticist movement.

items.title: Q46 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
"In every cry of every Man,
In every Infant's cry of fear,
In every voice, in every ban..."
The figure of speech characterized by repetition of words or group of words at the beginning
of consecutive sentences is called __________
items.explanation: Anaphora is a rhetorical figure of speech consisting of the deliberate repetition of a word or phrase ('In every...') at the beginning of successive clauses, sentences, or verse lines, as seen here in William Blake's poem 'London' (1794).

items.title: Q47 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit II: Poetry · Edmund Spenser
items.stem: At whose behest does the Redcrosse Knight undertake his quest in The Faerie Queene ?
items.explanation: As Edmund Spenser explains in Book I, Canto 1 and in his prefatory 'Letter to Sir Walter Raleigh' in The Faerie Queene (1590), the Redcrosse Knight undertakes his quest to slay the dragon and rescue Una's parents at the command of Gloriana, the Faerie Queene.

items.title: Q48 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit II: Poetry · John Ruskin
items.stem: In which city did John Ruskin see a paradigm for Victorian Britain ?
items.explanation: In his monumental three-volume architectural treatise The Stones of Venice (1851–1853), Victorian critic John Ruskin interpreted the rise and fall of the maritime empire of Venice—from pious Gothic craftsmanship to corrupt Renaissance luxury—as a moral warning and paradigm for industrial Victorian Britain.

items.title: Q49 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Kazuo Ishiguro
items.stem:
Which novel of Kazuo Ishiguro is narrated by a Japanese widow living in England and
draws on the destruction and rehabilitation of Nagasaki ?
items.explanation: Kazuo Ishiguro's debut novel A Pale View of Hills (1982) is narrated by Etsuko, a middle-aged Japanese widow living in England who reflects on her elder daughter Keiko's suicide while recalling her postwar memories of a rebuilding Nagasaki.

items.title: Q50 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem:
Which novel opens thus :
"Whether I shall turn out to be the hero of my own life, or whether that station will be held
by anyone else, these pages must show."
items.explanation: Charles Dickens's semi-autobiographical Bildungsroman David Copperfield (1849–1850) opens Chapter 1 ('I Am Born') with this famous sentence pondering whether the narrator himself will turn out to be the hero of his own life.

items.title: Q51 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: 15th-Century Transition, Drama & Early Print · Unit II: Poetry · Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.stem: Traces of the Morality plays are discernible in a play like Dr. Faustus, traces such as __________
options: its soliloquizing protagonist, Good and Bad Angels and its final moral
its refrains from the Corpus Christi Carol, the complaint of Christ, the lover of mankind
its rhythmical prose, and the presence of a larger narrative rhythm in the Morality plays
items.explanation: Christopher Marlowe's Renaissance tragedy Doctor Faustus (c. 1592) retains clear structural elements of the medieval English morality play, including a psychomachia struggle over the protagonist's soul between the Good Angel and the Evil (Bad) Angel, the Seven Deadly Sins, and the Chorus's closing moral warning.

items.title: Q52 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
The branch of philosophy that asks the question, 'How do we know what we know ?'
is __________
items.explanation: Epistemology (from the Greek episteme, 'knowledge') is the branch of philosophy that investigates the nature, origin, scope, and justification of human knowledge—asking 'How do we know what we know?'

items.title: Q53 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
The eighteenth century practice in England of bookselling was midway between direct
patronage and impersonal sales.  A patron paid half the cost of a book before publication
and half on delivery.  The author of the book received these payments directly.  The patron's
name appeared in the preface for the book published in this manner.
This practice was known as __________
items.explanation: Publication by subscription was a major eighteenth-century English publishing system—famously used by John Dryden for his Virgil and Alexander Pope for his Homer—in which subscribers paid half the price in advance and half upon delivery, with their names printed in a prefatory list.

items.title: Q54 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Oxford India has published a volume of Premchand translations in English, The Oxford India
Premchand.  Who among the following is not one of the translators ?
items.explanation: The Oxford India Premchand (2004), introduced by Francesca Orsini, brings together translations by David Rubin (The World of Premchand), Alok Rai (Nirmala), and Christopher R. King (Sons of the Soil), whereas Gillian Wright (translator of Rahi Masoom Raza and Shrilal Shukla) is not included.

items.title: Q55 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Jane Austen
items.stem:
Which of the two novels of Jane Austen have the spa town of Bath as a primary location ?
(a)
Emma
(b)
Pride and Prejudice
(c)
Northanger Abbey
(d)
Persuasion
The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: Jane Austen's posthumously published novels Northanger Abbey and Persuasion (both published together in December 1817, dated 1818) are both extensively set in the fashionable Georgian spa town of Bath, where Austen herself lived from 1801 to 1806.

items.title: Q56 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
In the communicative approach to ELT, the development of language learning or teaching
involves a shift :
(a)
from form-based to a meaning-based approach.
(b)
from an eclectic approach to a rigid method.
(c)
from teacher-centred to learner-centred classes.
(d)
from broad-based competence to specific needs.
The right combination, according to the Code is
items.explanation: Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) in English Language Teaching (ELT) involves a pedagogical shift from structural form-based drills to a meaning-based approach focused on real-world communication (a), and from teacher-dominated instruction to learner-centred classroom interaction (c).

items.title: Q57 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · Unit II: Poetry · Alexander Pope
items.stem:
The four Moral Essays of Alexander Pope are addressed to carefully selected figures.  Identify
the correct group
options: Lord Cobham, Robert Walpole, Houghton Hall, Chandos
Martha Blount, Lord Cobham, Bathurst, Burlington
William III, John Haydn, Joseph Addison, John Dennis
items.explanation: Alexander Pope's four Epistles to Several Persons (known as the Moral Essays, 1731–1735) are addressed respectively to Sir Richard Temple, Lord Cobham (Epistle I), a Lady—Martha Blount (Epistle II), Allen Lord Bathurst (Epistle III), and Richard Boyle, Earl of Burlington (Epistle IV).

items.title: Q58 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Bertolt Brecht's Mother Courage and Her Children presents the war-torn Europe as its
protagonist as she follows troops with her canteenwagon.
What is the real name of Mother Courage ?
items.explanation: In Bertolt Brecht's epic anti-war play Mother Courage and Her Children (Mutter Courage und ihre Kinder, 1939), set during the Thirty Years' War, the canteen-woman known as 'Mother Courage' is named Anna Fierling.

items.title: Q59 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
From among the following, identify the journal that publishes articles on English language
teaching and learning
items.explanation: TESOL Quarterly (Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages), founded in 1967, is a peer-reviewed international academic journal dedicated specifically to research in English language teaching and second language acquisition.

items.title: Q60 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit II: Poetry · Thomas Gray, Alfred Tennyson
items.stem: Arrange the following elegies in English in chronological order
options: Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" - "Adonais" - "Thyrsis" - "In Memoriam
Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" - "Adonais" - "In Memoriam" - "Thyrsis
Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" - "In Memoriam" - "Adonais" - "Thyrsis
Adonais" - "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" - "In Memoriam" - "Thyrsis
items.explanation: The chronological order of publication of these four famous English elegies is: Thomas Gray's 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' (1751), Percy Bysshe Shelley's 'Adonais' (1821), Alfred, Lord Tennyson's 'In Memoriam A.H.H.' (1850), and Matthew Arnold's 'Thyrsis' (1866).

items.title: Q61 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit II: Poetry · John Milton
items.stem: Who is the only one of Milton's contemporaries to be mentioned by name in Paradise Lost ?
items.explanation: Italian astronomer Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), whom John Milton visited near Florence in 1638, is the only contemporary of Milton mentioned in Paradise Lost (referred to as 'the Tuscan artist' in Book I, line 288, and by name as 'Galileo' in Book V, line 262).

items.title: Q62 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
K.S. Maniam is a major writer of Indian origin, writing in English, born and living in Malaysia.
Identify two of his novels from the following list.
(a)
The Rice Mother
(b)
The Return
(c)
Touching Earth
(d)
Between Lives
The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: Malaysian-Indian writer K. S. Maniam (1942–2020) is the author of the novels The Return (1981) (b) and Between Lives (2003) (d), whereas The Rice Mother (2002) is by Rani Manicka.

items.title: Q63 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: What did Thomas Percy collect in his Reliques ?
options: medieval folklore and lyrics of the Midlands
old songs, ballads, and romances in English and Scots
Highland lore, mostly oral wisdom of the Scots
items.explanation: Bishop Thomas Percy's three-volume anthology Reliques of Ancient English Poetry (1765), based on a seventeenth-century folio manuscript, collected old English and Scottish popular ballads, songs, metrical romances, and historical lyrics that inspired the Romantic ballad revival.

items.title: Q64 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Nirad Chaudhuri's Autobiography of an Unknown Indian concludes with an essay on the course
of Indian history.  But in the penultimate chapter Chaudhuri concludes the account of events
in his life.  How does this narrative end ?
options: Chaudhuri ties the knot with his childhood sweetheart and moves from Calcutta to Delhi
Chaudhuri obtains a job in the military accounts department and gives it up because he finds it soul-destroying
Chaudhuri joins the editorial team of a Calcutta newspaper and is upset over the drudgery of a reporter's life
Chaudhuri rushes to his ancestral village Bangram on receiving the news of the death of his uncle and recalls his past life
items.explanation: In the penultimate chapter ('Initiation into Scholarship') of The Autobiography of an Unknown Indian (1951), Nirad C. Chaudhuri recounts how after leaving his M.A. studies he entered the Military Accounts Department in Calcutta in 1921 as a clerk, only to find its bureaucratic drudgery soul-destroying.

items.title: Q65 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) · Unit II: Poetry · John Gower
items.stem:
In John Gower's Confessio Amantis, Amans, the lover makes his confession to the priest named
__________
items.explanation: In John Gower's Middle English poem Confessio Amantis (c. 1390), the aging lover Amans makes his confession of sins against love to Genius, the chaplain and priest of Venus, who illustrates the Seven Deadly Sins with exemplary tales.

items.title: Q66 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit I: Drama · Eugene Ionesco
items.stem:
In Eugene Ionesco's Chairs, the absurdity is not so much in the banal words that are uttered
as __________
options: in the large scale use of frightening stage props and lightning effects
in the absurdist interpretation of them by character after character
in the fact that they are spoken to an ever-growing number of empty chairs
in the fact that they are spoken time and again by members of the audience
items.explanation: In Eugène Ionesco's absurdist 'tragic farce' The Chairs (Les Chaises, 1952), an elderly couple franticly arrange an ever-multiplying number of empty chairs on stage to welcome an crowd of invisible guests, culminating in a deaf-mute Orator addressing the empty chairs.

items.title: Q67 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · Samuel Taylor Coleridge
items.stem:
A half-sentence in Purchas his Pilgrimage triggered off "Kubla Khan".  Whose work was
Purchas his Pilgrimage ?
options: John Hakluyt's, the collector of traveller's tales
items.explanation: In his 1816 preface to 'Kubla Khan', Samuel Taylor Coleridge explained that he fell into an opium-induced reverie in 1797 while reading a sentence about Kublai Khan's palace at Xandu in Purchas his Pilgrimage (1613), compiled by the English clergyman and travel writer Samuel Purchas.

items.title: Q68 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit II: Poetry · Robert Browning
items.stem:
Based on the life of a thirteenth-century troubadour, from among the following identify the
work, that marked a catastrophic failure in Robert Browning's poetic career, earning him a
reputation for impenetrable difficulty ?
items.explanation: Robert Browning's long narrative poem Sordello (1840), based on the thirteenth-century Mantuan troubadour Sordello da Goito mentioned in Dante's Purgatorio, was mocked by Victorian critics and readers for its extreme obscurity and severely damaged Browning's reputation for decades.

items.title: Q69 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Laurence Sterne
items.stem: In Tristram Shandy, the Author's preface __________
options: is hawked to the highest bidder
appears in-between chapters 13 and 14 in Volume II
is printed in italics in all editions
appears in-between chapters 10 and 11 in Volume I
items.explanation: In Laurence Sterne's Tristram Shandy (1759–1767), Sterne playfully subverts paratextual conventions: in Volume I, Chapters 8–9 he hawks his Dedication 'to the highest bidder' for fifty guineas, and he delays 'The Author's Preface' until Volume III, Chapter 20.

items.title: Q70 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · T. S. Eliot
items.stem:
Evelyn Waugh once complained that T.S. Eliot's Poems, 1909-1925 was "marvellously good,
but very hard to understand."  The most pessimistic novel Waugh wrote was called __________
and he owed the title to __________
options: Handful of Dust - The Waste Land
items.explanation: Evelyn Waugh took the title of his bleak, satirical novel of marital and spiritual collapse, A Handful of Dust (1934), from line 30 of Part I ('The Burial of the Dead') of T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land (1922): 'I will show you fear in a handful of dust.'

items.title: Q71 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
During the years 1830 to 1850, the illusion of peace in Victorian England was broken by such
incidents as ___________
options: Revolution in France and the Chartist Movement in England
General Strike of 1835 and the Rail Tragedy of 1847
the visionary libertarianism of poets and the lawless embodiment of revolution
the disaster of the Indian Mutiny and the incompetent bungling of the Crimean War
items.explanation: Between 1830 and 1850 (the 'Hungry Forties'), Victorian England's domestic peace was shaken by the working-class agitation of the Chartist Movement (1838–1848) at home and the revolutionary upheavals of the 1830 and 1848 Revolutions in France and continental Europe.

items.title: Q72 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Gulliver receives the following response when he boasts about his countrymen :
"... the most pernicious race of little odious vermin that nature ever suffered to crawl upon
the face of the earth."  Whose response ?
options: The first of the Houyhnhnms's he meets
items.explanation: In Part II, Chapter 6 of Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726), after Gulliver proudly describes English politics, wars, and institutions, the giant King of Brobdingnag delivers this devastating moral verdict on humanity as a 'pernicious race of little odious vermin'.

items.title: Q73 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
In the Inferno Dante, as he travels through the various circles of the hell finds Judas who is
unable to speak.  What is the reason behind this ?
options: His tongue is transformed into a coiled snake
His head is battered and so he cannot open his mouth
Lucifer is chewing on his head
His tongue is pulled out and nailed on the tree of sin
items.explanation: In Canto XXXIV of Dante Alighieri's Inferno, at the frozen centre of the ninth circle of Hell (Judecca), the three-faced giant Lucifer eternally chews the three arch-traitors—Judas Iscariot, Brutus, and Cassius—with Judas's head inside Lucifer's central mouth so he cannot speak.

items.title: Q74 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Assertion (A) :
Our reality is linguistic, a language mediated reality.
Reason (R)     :
Our perception and understanding of reality are largely constructed by the
words and other signs we use.
In the light of the statements above,
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
items.explanation: In structuralist and poststructuralist theory, both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and (R) directly explains (A): human reality is linguistically mediated precisely because our concepts, categories, and perceptions of the world are constructed through language and sign systems.

items.title: Q75 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: In his book, In Theory, Aijaz Ahmed works out the relations between the three entities
items.explanation: Marxist literary critic Aijaz Ahmad's influential book In Theory (1992) bears the subtitle 'Classes, Nations, Literatures', critiquing Fredric Jameson, Edward Said, and Salman Rushdie by analyzing how class structures, nation-states, and literary production intersect.

items.title: Q76 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
In 1660, a group of 12 people including Robert Boyle and Christopher Wren formed what
they called the Royal Society.  In 1663, it became The Royal Society of London for Improving
Natural Knowledge.  What was the Society's motto ?
options: In the words of no one
items.explanation: Founded in 1660, the Royal Society of London adopted the Latin motto 'Nullius in verba' (adapted from Horace's Epistles), which translates literally as 'in the words of no one' (or 'take nobody's word for it'), affirming empirical experimentation over scholastic authority.

items.title: Q77 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit II: Poetry · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: Of whom did W.B. Yeats say that "We were the last Romantics" ?
options: His Friends in the Irish Literary Revival
Himself and his lady love, Maud Gonne
items.explanation: In the final stanza of 'Coole Park and Ballylee, 1931' (published in The Winding Stair and Other Poems, 1933), W. B. Yeats declares, 'We were the last romantics—chose for theme / Traditional sanctity and loveliness,' referring to himself, Lady Augusta Gregory, and his fellow writers of the Irish Literary Revival.

items.title: Q78 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit II: Poetry · Thomas Gray
items.stem:
Who wrote The Wandering Jew, a poem in four cantos and the short lyric, "The Wandering
Jew's Soliloquy" ?
items.explanation: Romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792–1822) composed the early Gothic narrative poem The Wandering Jew in four cantos (with Thomas Medwin, c. 1809–1810) as well as the dramatic lyric 'The Wandering Jew's Soliloquy'.

items.title: Q79 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Where, according to T.S. Eliot, are we likely to find "not only the best, but the most individual
parts of a poet's work" ?
options: in the poet's juvenilia or rejected drafts
in the best anthologies and scrap-books
in those parts where the dead poets assert their immortality
in those parts where the living poets depart from their ancestors
items.explanation: In his seminal essay 'Tradition and the Individual Talent' (1919), T. S. Eliot writes that if we approach a poet without prejudice looking for what is individual, we shall often find that 'not only the best, but the most individual parts of his work may be those in which the dead poets, his ancestors, assert their immortality most vigorously'.

items.title: Q80 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) · Unit II: Poetry · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Which of the following is true of The Canterbury Tales ?
options: Chaucer, the pilgrim, narrates Sir Thopas' Tale only
Chaucer, the pilgrim, narrates The Tale of Melibee only
Chaucer, the pilgrim, narrates both Sir Thopas' Tale and The Tale of Melibee
Chaucer, the pilgrim does attempt to narrate an unnamed tale but abruptly stops due to the intervention of the other pilgrims
items.explanation: In Fragment VII of Geoffrey Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales, Chaucer's pilgrim persona first narrates the burlesque tail-rhyme romance 'The Tale of Sir Thopas' until the Host Harry Bailly interrupts his 'drasty rymyng', whereupon Chaucer narrates the long moral prose treatise 'The Tale of Melibee'.

items.title: Q81 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
During the reign of Norman Kings, it was fashionable to speak __________ in upper-class
circles in England
items.explanation: Following the Norman Conquest of 1066, Norman French (Anglo-Norman) became the prestigious language of the royal court, nobility, law, and polite upper-class society in England for over two centuries.

items.title: Q82 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Aldous Huxley
items.stem:
Who, among the following, collaborated with Purohit Swami in translating the Ten Principal
Upanishads into English ?
items.explanation: In 1935–1936 in Majorca and London, Irish poet W. B. Yeats collaborated closely with Indian monk Shree Purohit Swami to translate The Ten Principal Upanishads into clear, idiomatic English (published by Faber and Faber in 1937).

items.title: Q83 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit II: Poetry · Ben Jonson
items.stem:
What unique distinction does Ben Jonson's "To Penshurst" have in the English literary
canon ?
options: It is the only distinguished poem in English addressed to the Lords of Penshurst
It celebrates Philip Sidney's elevation to knighthood, Sidney being the youngest scion of the family
It is one of the first English poems celebrating a specific place, a forerunner to Cooper's Hill and Windsor-Forest
It is the first poem in an elegiac series that late Elizabethan poets began on the demise of the Lord of Penshurst
items.explanation: Ben Jonson's 'To Penshurst' (published in The Forrest in his 1616 Folio Workes), praising the Kentish estate of Sir Robert Sidney, inaugurated the seventeenth-century English 'country-house' and topographical poem tradition later followed by John Denham's Cooper's Hill and Alexander Pope's Windsor-Forest.

items.title: Q84 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Tom Stoppard, E. M. Forster
items.stem:
It is well known that in many of his plays, Tom Stoppard has consciously drawn upon
earlier, often reputed, works.  Match the following Stoppard plays with earlier works whose
spirit seems to have informed them.
(a)
Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead
(i)
Hamlet
(b)
Indian Ink
(ii)
A Passage to India
(c)
Inspector Hound
(iii)
The Mousetrap
(d)
Travesties
(iv)
Importance of Being Earnest
Code :
(a)
(b)
(c)
(d)
items.explanation: Tom Stoppard's intertextual plays draw on earlier classics: (a) Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead (1966) reworks Shakespeare's Hamlet (i); (b) Indian Ink (1995) echoes E. M. Forster's A Passage to India (ii); (c) The Real Inspector Hound (1968) parodies Agatha Christie's The Mousetrap (iii); and (d) Travesties (1974) is structured around Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest (iv).

items.stem:
After discovering the truth about his heinous crimes committed in the past, what does Oedipus
request as his punishment ?
items.explanation: At the climax of Sophocles's tragedy Oedipus Rex, after discovering that he has unwittingly killed his father Laius and married his mother Jocasta, Oedipus gouges out his own eyes with Jocasta's golden brooches and begs Creon to banish him into exile from Thebes.

items.title: Q86 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · D. H. Lawrence
items.stem: How does Women in Love open ?
options: Rupert Birkin, Lawrence's alter ego, is taking a walk in the English Countryside
The Brangwen sisters, Ursula and Gudrun, are "working and talking
The wedding party gathers at shortlands, the Criches's home
The last lesson is in progress, "peaceful and still" in Ursula's classroom
items.explanation: D. H. Lawrence's novel Women in Love (1920) opens in Chapter 1 ('Sisters') at the Brangwen home in Beldover, where the sisters Ursula and Gudrun Brangwen are sitting together 'working and talking' about marriage before walking to the Crich wedding.

items.title: Q87 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Samuel Johnson
items.stem:
Samuel Johnson has the following to say about an English poet :
"These images are marked by glittering accumulations of ungraceful ornaments : they strike,
rather than please.  The images are magnified by affectation : the language is laboured into
harshness.  The mind of the writer seems to work  with unnatural violence - 'Double, double,
toil and trouble'.  He has a kind of strutting dignity, and is tall by walking on tiptoe.  His art
and his struggle are too visible, and there is too little appearance of ease and nature."
Identify the poet
items.explanation: In his 'Life of Gray' from Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets (1781), Samuel Johnson harshly criticized Thomas Gray's Pindaric odes ('The Progress of Poesy' and 'The Bard') for artificial diction and strained sublimity, remarking that Gray 'has a kind of strutting dignity, and is tall by walking on tiptoe'.

items.title: Q88 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
"Take the smoking disclaimer issue" begins Vishal Bharadwaj.  "Putting a disclaimer every
time somebody smokes on screen is not an answer.  If M.F. Hussain had painted a man with
a cigar, would you have asked him to put the disclaimer, 'Cigarette smoking is injurious to
health' on the painting" ?
The point Bharadwaj makes with his rhetorical question is the following
options: The smoking disclaimer is ineffectual because M.F. Hussain's painting wouldn't have carried it
The smoking disclaimer on objects perceived as 'art' is simply superfluous
The smoking disclaimer is ineffectual because 'art' entertains but does not instruct
The smoking disclaimer on screen or on an M.F. Hussain painting distracts us from enjoying art
items.explanation: Through his rhetorical analogy comparing cinema to an M. F. Husain painting of a man smoking a cigar, filmmaker Vishal Bhardwaj argues that mandatory health disclaimers superimposed onto works of art are intrusive and superfluous.

items.title: Q89 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: According to __________, certain verbs actually 'perform' an act when they are uttered
options: Speech Act theorists such as Austin and Searle
Russian Formalists such as Shklovsky and Propp
Language theorists such as Sapir and Whorf
Cognitive linguists such as Lakoff and Johnson
items.explanation: In Speech Act Theory, pioneered by Oxford philosopher J. L. Austin in How to Do Things with Words (1962) and developed by John Searle, 'performative utterances' (such as 'I promise', 'I apologize', or 'I pronounce you') actually perform an action in the very act of being spoken.

items.title: Q90 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Haunted castles, strange noises, and an acceptance of the supernatural with all its trappings
mark __________
items.explanation: Inaugurated by Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto (1764) and popularized by Ann Radcliffe and Matthew Gregory Lewis, Gothic fiction is characterized by medieval haunted castles, subterranean passages, mysterious noises, brooding villains, and supernatural terror.

items.title: Q92 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Arrange the following plays of Shakespeare according to their periods (early, middle, late...)
of composition
options: You Like It, Love's Labours Lost, Antony and Cleopatra, The Tempest, Midsummer Night's Dream
Antony and Cleopatra, The Tempest, Midsummer Night's Dream, Love's Labours Lost, As You Like It
Love's Labours Lost, Midsummer Night's Dream, As You Like It, Antony and Cleopatra, The Tempest
Midsummer Night's Dream, Antony and Cleopatra, The Tempest, As You Like It, Love's Labours Lost
items.explanation: Arranged chronologically from Shakespeare's early to late periods of composition, the plays are: Love's Labour's Lost (c. 1594), A Midsummer Night's Dream (c. 1595–1596), As You Like It (c. 1599), Antony and Cleopatra (c. 1606–1607), and his late romance The Tempest (c. 1611).

items.title: Q93 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem: Who among the following is not a reader-response critic ?
items.explanation: While Hans-Robert Jauss, Wolfgang Iser (Constance School reception theory), and Stanley Fish (affective stylistics) are major reader-response theorists, British scholar Maud Bodkin (1875–1967) was a pioneer of Jungian archetypal criticism, famous for Archetypal Patterns in Poetry (1934).

items.title: Q94 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Leo Tolstoy
items.stem: Leo Tolstoy's Anna Karenina's closing lines present
options: a sad reflection on the unfortunate suicide of Anna which should have been averted
the enlivening freshness of a rain which has been threatening to break out
Levin's affirmation that whatever happens to him, life is not meaningless but unquestionably meaningful
Vronsky's lament over the death of Anna which ends on a positive note, affirming the human tendency to pass over the tragic events with hope
items.explanation: Leo Tolstoy's novel Anna Karenina (1877) does not end with Anna's suicide in Part VII, but continues through Part VIII, concluding with Konstantin Levin's spiritual epiphany under the starry sky that his life now has an 'unquestionable meaning of the good which I have the power to put into it'.

items.title: Q95 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Wilkie Collins
items.stem:
Which of the following novels begins with a Prologue under the title "The Storming of
Seringapatam", saying "I address these lines written in India - to my relatives in England" ?
options: The Siege of Krishnapur by J.G. Farell
The Sign of Four by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle
The Jewel in the Crown by Paul Scott
items.explanation: Wilkie Collins's detective novel The Moonstone (1868) opens with a Prologue titled 'The Storming of Seringapatam (1799). Extracted from a Family Paper', in which an English officer recounts how his cousin John Herncastle looted the sacred yellow diamond in India.

items.title: Q96 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
In "Gerontion", T.S. Eliot says :
"__________ has many cunning passages, contrived corridors / And issues, deceives with
whispering ambitions, / Guides us by vanities."
What is Eliot's subject ?
items.explanation: In T. S. Eliot's dramatic monologue 'Gerontion' (published in Ara Vos Prec, 1920), the aging speaker meditates on the deceptive, labyrinthine nature of human history: 'After such knowledge, what forgiveness? Think now / History has many cunning passages, contrived corridors / And issues, deceives with whispering ambitions, / Guides us by vanities.'

items.title: Q97 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Whose poetic voice is triggered right from the beginning ?
items.explanation: American poet Louise Glück's poem 'The Mountain' (from A Village Life, 2009) opens directly in the first-person voice of a poetry teacher addressing a classroom ('My students look at me expectantly. / I explain to them that the life of art is a life / of endless labor').

items.title: Q98 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: The speaker brings up the story of Sisyphus specifically by way of glossing __________
items.explanation: In Louise Glück's poem 'The Mountain', the teacher-speaker invokes the Greek myth of Sisyphus rolling his boulder up the mountain specifically to gloss and illustrate the concept of 'endless labor' in the life of art.

items.title: Q99 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
In its context, the words "their fingers / tapping at the wooden desks", best represent the
students' __________
items.explanation: In Louise Glück's 'The Mountain', as the teacher lectures on Sisyphus's eternal toil, the students' 'fingers / tapping at the wooden desks' and their glancing out the window represent their restless boredom and show of impatience.

items.title: Q100 · July 2018 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Why does the speaker say that "the rock has added height to the mountain" ?
options: because the speaker is already on the top of the mountain
because both the hands of the speaker are now free
because the mountain now seems largely incomprehensible
because she feels that the immensity of the problem has grown. - o O o
items.explanation: At the end of Louise Glück's 'The Mountain', the speaker's observation that 'the rock has added height to the mountain' signifies that the ongoing weight of artistic and existential struggle has only magnified the immensity of the task ahead.
